items.title: Cutting an integral into 100 trapezoids beats analytical integration for most real problems
items.claim: Most integrals appearing in physics, engineering or statistics do NOT have closed-form solutions. They're computed numerically. The simplest method (trapezoidal rule) divides the interval into strips and approximates each as a trapezoid.

options.text: Error in the trapezoidal rule is O(1/n^2) where n is the number of strips. Simpson's rule (quadratic interpolation) is O(1/n^4). Gauss-Legendre and adaptive quadrature can achieve essentially machine precision for well-behaved integrands
Always less accurate than analytical answers

items.reveal:
Trapezoidal rule: approximate integral from a to b of f(x) dx by the sum of trapezoidal strips. Error scales as h^2 (where h is the strip width), so halving h quarters the error.

Simpson's rule (uses quadratic fits to triples of points): error scales as h^4. Halving h reduces error by 16x.

For a function smooth enough on [a, b], Simpson's rule with 20 strips can give 6-7 decimal places of accuracy. Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 10 nodes can give 10-15 decimal places.

Many real-world integrals:
- integral of e^(-x^2) dx: no elementary antiderivative. Used everywhere in statistics. Always computed numerically (or via the error function erf).
- integral of sin(x)/x dx: no elementary form. Defined as the sine integral Si(x).
- integral over irregular domains, multidimensional integrals, integrals with singularities — numerical methods are standard.

Monte Carlo integration: for high-dimensional integrals (d > ~4), grid-based methods (Simpson, Gauss) suffer the 'curse of dimensionality' — n grid points per axis means n^d total. Monte Carlo (random sampling) has error O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of dimension; the standard tool for integrals in 10+ dimensions (e.g., statistical mechanics, finance).

More sophisticated: adaptive quadrature (refines where the function is wiggly), Romberg's method, Chebyshev quadrature for analytic functions, sparse grids, quasi-Monte Carlo with low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton).

The trade-off between numerical and analytical: analytical is exact when available, but unavailable for most functions. Numerical is universally applicable, with accuracy dialed up by computational cost.
items.why: Calculus class focuses on analytical integration. Real applied math is largely numerical — and the numerical methods can be vastly faster and more accurate than the analytical ones for the integrals actually needed.

items.title: The simplest population equation in the world becomes chaotic
items.claim: Logistic map: x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n). At r = 2.5, x converges to a fixed point. At r = 3.2, it oscillates between two values. At r = 3.7, the values look random. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.

options.text: Nothing — the system is always periodic

Period-doubling cascade: a single fixed point splits into a 2-cycle, then a 4-cycle, then 8, 16, 32... at geometrically closer values of r (Feigenbaum's constant ~4.669). Beyond ~3.5699, the system becomes chaotic
Only mathematicians can see the difference
The chaos is a calculation error

items.reveal_title: Period doubling and the road to chaos
items.reveal:
The logistic map x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n) was introduced by Robert May (1976) as a simple model of population growth with carrying capacity.

For r between 0 and 1: x converges to 0.
For r between 1 and 3: x converges to a non-zero fixed point.
At r = 3: the fixed point becomes unstable; period-2 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.449: period-4 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.544: period-8.
At r ≈ 3.5644: period-16.

The period-doublings occur at geometrically closer r-values, with ratio approaching Feigenbaum's constant delta ≈ 4.669 — a universal constant of period-doubling bifurcations, appearing in many physical systems (dripping faucet, electronic circuits, fluid dynamics).

At r ≈ 3.5699: 'Edge of chaos'. Beyond this, the system becomes chaotic — small differences in initial conditions grow exponentially.

Within the chaos there are 'islands of stability' (e.g., a period-3 window near r ≈ 3.83). The bifurcation diagram has fractal structure.

This system shows that deterministic dynamics can produce apparent randomness. It motivated chaos theory in the 1970s-80s.

Applications:
- Population biology (when not too realistic).
- Cryptography (pseudo-random number generators).
- Modelling complex systems (transitions to turbulence).
- Analogies to neural and economic dynamics.

The logistic map is a foundational example in the study of dynamical systems and has become a textbook reference for chaos.
items.why: Even the simplest equations can produce unpredictable behaviour. Determinism doesn't guarantee predictability — chaos can emerge from one-line iterations. This insight overturned 19th-century certainty about Newtonian mechanics.

items.title: Half the world's billionaires got there partly by luck
items.claim: Repeated coin flips produce some very lucky streaks. The proportion of 'successful' (still in business, in market, alive) entities at the top of a population sample is dominated by selection effects — the unsuccessful disappear from view, leaving the survivors looking exceptional.

options.text: Survivorship bias: we only see the successes, and infer skill from outcomes; randomness alone would have produced some 'winners' from a starting pool, but we don't see the matching losers

items.reveal_title: Survivorship bias and the law of large pools
items.reveal:
If 10,000 hedge fund managers each pick stocks randomly for 10 years, about (1/1024) * 10,000 ≈ 10 will have called the market right 10 years running (by pure luck). These 10 will be on the cover of business magazines, will publish books on their 'secrets', and will attract investor billions.

The other 9,990 are out of business and forgotten.

Mochon and Norton (2011, 2012) replicated this in the lab: random stock-picking among 'subjects' produced 'expert' track records statistically indistinguishable from actual hedge funds. Selection of survivors creates the illusion of skill.

Real-world cases:
- WWII US bombers: aircraft returning from missions had bullet holes in wings and fuselage, not engines or cockpits. The Air Force initially considered reinforcing where the holes were — until Abraham Wald pointed out: planes hit in the engine or cockpit don't return. Reinforce the unhit areas.
- Famous 'success stories' (Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, J.K. Rowling) tell entrepreneurs what to do — but tens of thousands who tried the same things failed.
- Stock market: survivor-bias-corrected returns are ~1-2% per year lower than uncorrected indices, because failed stocks drop out.

The correct statistical question is not 'what did successful X do?' but 'what's the base rate of success among everyone who tried that?'.
items.why: Success seems instructive. Survivorship bias means we systematically learn from outliers and ignore the (invisible) ordinary cases. The math of selection effects is more important than the stories of any individual.
